general.temas: The election campaign and the debate between Sánchez and Feijóo dominate the front pages, with attention to the polls, party reactions and the PSOE’s strategy. The suspension of voting rights for people naturalized under the grandchildren law and the PP’s immigration proposals also feature repeatedly. Only ABC highlights the rapprochement between the EU and the United Kingdom to reverse Brexit.
general.motivo_crispacion: The campaign is marked by high tension between the PP and the PSOE following the head-to-head debate, with accusations of insults and lies and criticism of Sánchez’s performance. There are also clashes between left-wing parties and controversy over the suspension of voting rights for thousands of naturalized citizens. Immigration and border control add sensitive issues to the political debate. By contrast, sports, food and technology stories offer calmer content.

El País.resumen:
- The gap between the PP and the PSOE is narrowing, even though Feijóo won the debate according to the poll cited.
- The campaign includes a Sánchez rally in Galicia and Feijóo’s proposals on immigration and security.
- The front page covers reactions to the debate, fact-checking of claims and the candidates’ body language.
- Podemos brings supporters together in Madrid, while the Supreme Court keeps in place the suspension of voting rights for 163,000 people naturalized under the grandchildren law.
- A slump in companies linked to artificial intelligence drags the Nasdaq to its worst week in a year and a half.
El País.motivo_populismo: The tone is predominantly informative, although expressions such as “gets his revenge,” “flex their muscles” and “the bloodbath” add drama and present events as a contest.
El País.sesgo: The selection focuses on the electoral contest, the polls and the debate between Sánchez and Feijóo. The comparison of attendance figures favors Sánchez’s image, while the focus on Feijóo emphasizes the tough tone of his immigration rhetoric.

El Mundo.resumen:
- Election tracking puts Feijóo at his best polling figure of the campaign, while Sánchez narrows the gap with the PP.
- The front page features reactions to the debate, criticism of Sánchez and a rapprochement between Abascal and Feijóo.
- The Supreme Court demands compliance with the order barring 163,355 people naturalized under the grandchildren law from voting, with exceptions.
- Morocco blocks work on the Ceuta breakwater for several hours; it later resumes.
- Spain’s decree on data centers, Trump’s warnings and AI-related stock market falls feature prominently, alongside sports news.
El Mundo.motivo_populismo: Expressions such as “revenge,” “he ate him alive” and “fateful week” add drama and confrontation, although there is no clear appeal to the people against the elites.
El Mundo.sesgo: The front page prioritizes the election campaign and presents several stories from a perspective critical of Sánchez, although it also covers his rise in the poll and his attacks on Feijóo. The selection and wording emphasize the competition between parties and reactions to the debate.

ABC.resumen:
- Allegations about Jensen Huang, his personal life and his working methods are recounted.
- Olympiacos defeats Real Madrid in the EuroLeague.
- Two minors steal a bus in Italy to imitate a video game and crash.
- The front page covers the debate between Sánchez and Feijóo, a Podemos rally and the PP’s border proposals.
- The EU and the United Kingdom agree on a rapprochement; there is also food content and recipes.
ABC.motivo_populismo: Expressions such as “tears apart,” “takes by storm” and “woman trouble,” along with the threat quoted in the first headline, add drama and sensationalism, although there is no discernible general appeal to the people against the elites.
ABC.sesgo: The debate coverage presents Feijóo as having been boosted by the encounter and emphasizes disappointment within the PSOE, encouraging a positive interpretation for the PP. The text about Podemos resorts to stereotypes about its events and attendees.

Público.resumen:
- The PSOE enters the final stretch of the campaign on the rise, but without a majority to govern against the PP and Vox.
- A post-debate poll puts the PSOE less than one point behind the PP; the head-to-head drew ten million viewers.
- Several headlines feature criticism and mockery of Feijóo over his statements in the debate.
- The front page suggests that euthanasia could be at risk under a PP-Vox government.
- The Supreme Court prevents 163,000 people naturalized under the “grandchildren law” from voting, according to the front page.
Público.motivo_populismo: Expressions such as “devastating,” “falsehoods” and “burst out laughing,” together with the warning that euthanasia “could be lost,” introduce an emotional and confrontational tone.
Público.sesgo: The selection and wording show a particularly critical approach to Feijóo and a possible PP-Vox government, while emphasizing the PSOE’s rise in the polls. They also include Montero and Rufián’s demand that the PSOE be “supervised.”

OKdiario.resumen:
- The election campaign accounts for several headlines about Sánchez, Feijóo and PP leaders.
- Pérez-Reverte warns about the security of Ceuta and Melilla in the event of a possible crisis with Morocco.
- La Liga returns with Barcelona and Real Madrid fighting for the lead; there is also news about football and motorcycle racing.
- Samsung confirms smart glasses with Gemini, and Torres Quevedo’s contribution to automation is recalled.
- Madrid replaces Naviluz with a new route for viewing the Christmas lights.
OKdiario.motivo_populismo: Expressions such as “flounder,” “defends himself” and “unprecedented” add drama and disparagement, although there is no discernible explicit appeal to the people against the elites.
OKdiario.sesgo: The political selection and wording show an approach favorable to the PP and critical of Pedro Sánchez, whose defeat in the debate is presented as fact. The headlines about Moreno and Miranda highlight the success of an event and criticism of the government, respectively.

opiniones.comunista:
I do not judge a campaign by who wins a debate, but by what it proposes for people who live from their work. The PP’s promise to use the armed forces in response to immigration turns migrants into a security problem. In my view, that policy divides the working class and diverts attention from the economic power that shapes everyone’s lives.

I also see the debate over data centers as a dispute over control of the economy. It is not enough to measure their value by private investment: we must ask whom they serve and who decides. I support strong public services and collective ownership of strategic infrastructure, so that their benefits meet social needs rather than merely serving the profitability of big capital. Democracy must extend to the economy too.
opiniones.anarquista:
I see the campaign once again reducing politics to a fight between candidates and fractions of a point in the polls. I do not dismiss the consequences of who governs, but I distrust a democracy that invites us to delegate power and wait. The parties compete for control; I prefer to build decision-making capacity from the bottom up, through assemblies and mutual aid networks.

I am particularly concerned about the promise to deploy armed forces in response to immigration: turning borders into a military issue does not address the needs of the people arriving or those receiving them. I also oppose leaving thousands of naturalized citizens without a vote: that exclusion reveals the extent to which the state decides who counts. Freedom should not depend on a hierarchy, but be sustained collectively, without anyone losing their autonomy.
opiniones.liberal:
I see too much attention paid to the winner of the debate and too little to the freedom we will have after the election. The decree on data centers deserves rigorous scrutiny: regulation is not cost-free if it adds obstacles that discourage investment. I prefer clear rules, low taxes and a limited state that protects rights rather than deciding for businesses and citizens.

I also disagree with Trump’s threat to penalize companies that build data centers outside the United States with taxes. The freedom to invest and trade should not depend on political borders. That said, the free market requires responsibility: companies must bear their own risks, including when stock markets fall, without demanding that taxpayers pay for their mistakes. And individual freedom matters just as much at the end of life: I believe each person should be able to decide without others imposing their wishes.
opiniones.extrema_derecha:
I care less about who won the debate than about who is willing to genuinely defend Spain’s sovereignty. The promise to strengthen borders and call on the Armed Forces when national security requires it points in the right direction, but announcing it on the campaign trail is not enough. I want effective controls, demanding cooperation with countries of origin and an immigration policy decided by Spaniards, not dictated by criminal gangs or pressure from elites far removed from our borders.

The incident at the construction site in Ceuta requires the facts to be clarified and our interests to be defended firmly, without recklessness or hasty concessions. And in the euthanasia debate, I stand for a society that cares for its elderly and sick and protects life. Polls and televised gestures should not obscure these fundamental decisions.
opiniones.centro:
I see a campaign too preoccupied with who won the debate and too little concerned with which policies can build lasting support. Firmness is not incompatible with precision: I expect verifiable proposals from the candidates and a willingness to compromise. On immigration, protecting borders is legitimate, but calling on the Armed Forces requires justification of their necessity and respect for legal and humanitarian safeguards. The Canary Islands need practical responses, not just campaign gestures.

I am also concerned about the suspension of voting rights for thousands of naturalized citizens. I respect the Supreme Court’s decision, but I believe institutions should explain its grounds and facilitate access to the available avenues of appeal for those who consider themselves adversely affected. And on data centers, I prefer predictable regulation, discussed with the sector and compatible with investment, to turning every regulation into a promise of repeal. Moving forward through agreements may be less flashy, but it offers greater stability.
